nodes.title: Observed rain (radar + gauges)
nodes.plain: Radar plus rain gauges tell us how much rain fell on every 1 km square, every hour.
nodes.what: NOAA MRMS MultiSensor QPE 01H Pass2: radar precipitation bias-corrected with rain gauges. Before 14 Oct 2020 the gauge-corrected GaugeCorr QPE (IEM archive); RadarOnly only as a last resort, recorded per hour.

source.text: NOAA NSSL / NCEP, MRMS MultiSensor QPE 01H Pass2 (AWS noaa-mrms-pds)
Zhang J. et al. (2016) Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) quantitative precipitation estimation. BAMS 97(4)

nodes.how_used: Bilinear interpolation onto the 20 m cell centres; drives storm replays and the 12 h spin-up of every forecast.
nodes.output: rain r(x, y, t), mm per hour on 20 m cells
nodes.limits: Radar under-reads in the heaviest convective cores and far from the radar; gauges are sparse.

nodes.title: Forecast rain + 2 m temperature (HRRR)
nodes.plain: A weather-forecast model says how much rain will fall in the next two days, every hour, on 3 km squares.
nodes.what: NOAA HRRR v4 hourly precipitation buckets (APCP) and 2 m air temperature; 48 h cycles at 00/06/12/18 UTC, 18 h cycles every hour.

source.text: NOAA GSL / NCEP, High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) v4 (AWS noaa-hrrr-bdp-pds)
Dowell D.C. et al. (2022) The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR): an hourly updating convection-allowing forecast model. Part I. Weather and Forecasting 37(8)

nodes.how_used: Forecast rain on the 20 m grid after neighbourhood spreading; the temperature splits rain from snow.
nodes.output: forecast rain and temperature fields per forecast hour
nodes.limits: A 3 km forecast cannot place a thunderstorm to the street; storms are often displaced by tens of km.

nodes.title: Ground height (lidar)
nodes.plain: Laser scans from aircraft measured the height of the ground everywhere, so we know which way water runs.
nodes.what: USGS 3DEP lidar-derived bare-earth DEM at 10 m (tiles), quality level 2.

source.text: USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), 1/3 arc-second and lidar-derived 10 m DEM
USGS Lidar Base Specification (quality level 2: RMSEz ≤ 10 cm)

nodes.how_used: Averaged to the 20 m model grid; its highest 10 m cell per 20 m cell is kept as the road crest.
nodes.limits: Bare earth hides pipes and culverts under roads; bridges and decks are removed.

nodes.title: Streams (NHDPlus HR)
nodes.plain: A national map of every stream and river tells us where water channels already exist.
nodes.what: USGS NHDPlus HR flowlines with drainage area; bankfull width and depth from regional curves.

source.text: USGS NHDPlus High Resolution
Bieger K., Rathjens H., Allen P.M., Arnold J.G. (2015) Development and evaluation of bankfull hydraulic geometry relationships for the physiographic regions of the United States. JAWRA 51(3)

nodes.how_used: Flowline cells are carved to bankfull depth so rivers carry their water in the model.
nodes.limits: Small ditches and piped streams are missing or misplaced.

nodes.title: Soils (SSURGO)
nodes.plain: Soil maps say how quickly the ground can soak up rain: sandy soil drinks fast, clay slowly.
nodes.what: USDA NRCS SSURGO hydrologic soil group A–D (and shallow water table → D).

source.text: USDA NRCS Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO), hydrologic soil group

nodes.how_used: Sets the curve number of every cell together with land cover.
nodes.limits: Map units are coarse; soil changes within a few metres are not resolved.

nodes.title: Land cover + pavement (NLCD 2021)
nodes.plain: Satellite maps say which ground is forest, grass or pavement; pavement makes almost all rain run off.
nodes.what: MRLC NLCD 2021 land-cover classes and fractional impervious surface.

source.text: MRLC National Land Cover Database 2021 (land cover + fractional impervious surface)

nodes.how_used: Impervious share → curve number and Manning roughness.
nodes.limits: 30 m pixels blur narrow streets and parking lots.

nodes.title: Roads (MassDOT Road Inventory)
nodes.plain: The state road list gives every road piece, how big it is and how many cars use it per day.
nodes.what: MassDOT Road Inventory: District 3 road graph (segments, functional class, speed, AADT, connectivity).

source.text: MassDOT Road Inventory (segments, functional class, AADT) via the MassDOT open-data portal

nodes.how_used: Road points every 10 m are sampled on the depth grid; the graph carries detours and access.
nodes.limits: Some AADT values are defaults; private roads and driveways are not in the inventory.

nodes.title: Culverts and stream crossings
nodes.plain: A list of every place where a road crosses a stream, with the pipe size and condition where it was surveyed.
nodes.what: Road–stream crossings from the MA Stream Crossings Project / NAACC surveys (size, shape, condition, inlet blockage), USGS/TIGER road–stream intersections, MassDOT structures and the NBI (bridges).

source.text: North Atlantic Aquatic Connectivity Collaborative (NAACC) road-stream crossing surveys
Massachusetts Stream Crossings / UMass Stream Continuity Project
FHWA National Bridge Inventory

nodes.how_used: Opens a notch through the road fill at each crossing; sizes the HDS-5 culvert check; bridges stay open.
nodes.limits: Only part of the crossings have a surveyed size or condition.

nodes.title: People (2020 Census blocks)
nodes.plain: The Census tells us how many people live on each block, so we can count who gets cut off.
nodes.what: 2020 Census blocks, population at each block internal point.

source.text: US Census Bureau, 2020 Census blocks (TIGER/Line + P1 population)

nodes.how_used: Each block is attached to its nearest road segment.
nodes.limits: Night-time (home) population only.

nodes.title: Hospitals, fire, police
nodes.plain: Where the hospitals, fire stations and police stations are, so we can check who can still reach them.
nodes.what: OpenStreetMap hospitals, fire stations, police (Overpass extract, Oct 2026).

source.text: OpenStreetMap contributors (hospitals, fire and police stations, via Overpass)

nodes.how_used: Sources of the shortest-path searches for emergency access.
nodes.limits: OSM completeness varies; no staffing or capacity data.

nodes.title: 20 m terrain grid
nodes.plain: The ground heights are averaged into 20 m squares, a 1000 × 1000 grid for each 20 km box.
nodes.what: 10 m DEM tiles averaged to RES = 20 m; each run covers a 20 × 20 km box in EPSG:26986 (MA State Plane, m).

source.text: USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), 1/3 arc-second and lidar-derived 10 m DEM

nodes.output: z(x, y), m on 20 m cells
nodes.limits: A 20 m cell cannot hold a gutter or curb line (< 1 m wide).

nodes.title: Rivers carved to bankfull
nodes.plain: Rivers are dug into the grid so they can carry water the way real channels do.
nodes.what: NHDPlus HR flowline cells lowered by a volume-equivalent bankfull burn; with the live terrain fix, flowlines (incl. buried conduits) are enforced as continuous downhill conveyance.

source.text: USGS NHDPlus High Resolution
Bieger K., Rathjens H., Allen P.M., Arnold J.G. (2015) Development and evaluation of bankfull hydraulic geometry relationships for the physiographic regions of the United States. JAWRA 51(3)

parameters.name: maximum enforcement cut
parameters.origin: set by us (cap against DEM artefacts)

nodes.limits: Bankfull geometry from regional curves, not surveyed.

nodes.title: Road–stream crossing notch (3 × 3 cells)
nodes.plain: Where a stream goes under a road, we cut a small gap in the road so the water can pass, like the real pipe.
nodes.what: At every mapped crossing a 3 × 3-cell notch is cut through the road fill to the lowest ground within 40 m; with the live fix, levels are read from the un-notched DEM and the notch is joined to its outlet.

source.text: North Atlantic Aquatic Connectivity Collaborative (NAACC) road-stream crossing surveys
Massachusetts Stream Crossings / UMass Stream Continuity Project

nodes.how_used: Stands in for the culvert barrel (the model has no pipes).

parameters.name: search radius for the notch level
parameters.origin: set by us (two cells each side)

nodes.limits: A notch passes far more water than a small or blocked pipe; stream water in the notch can read as road depth (handled by the rain-onset rule).

nodes.title: Pit breaching (ponds kept)
nodes.plain: Fake holes in the ground map are opened so water can drain; real ponds deeper than 4 m are kept.
nodes.what: Least-cost breaching of every closed depression to the box edge (Barnes et al. 2014 priority-flood with carving), 4-connected (the solver exchanges water across cell faces).

source.text: Barnes R., Lehman C., Mulla D. (2014) Priority-flood: an optimal depression-filling and watershed-labeling algorithm for digital elevation models. Computers & Geosciences 62

parameters.name: maximum cut
parameters.origin: set by us (deeper basins are real ponds / quarries)

parameters.name: 4-connected carving
parameters.origin: set by us (LISFLOOD-FP exchanges water across faces only)

nodes.limits: A carved one-cell path is a stand-in for an unknown pipe.

nodes.title: Road-crest height
nodes.plain: We remember the highest point of the ground in each square, which is usually the road top.
nodes.what: Highest 10 m lidar cell inside each 20 m cell (z_raw_max10), before any hydraulic edit; bridge decks read depth from their approaches.

source.text: USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), 1/3 arc-second and lidar-derived 10 m DEM

nodes.how_used: Freeboard and overtopping checks, crest-relative depth near crossings.
nodes.limits: Lidar RMSEz ≈ 0.10 m.

nodes.title: Runoff: curve number (TR-55)
nodes.plain: For each square we work out how much of the rain runs off instead of soaking in.
nodes.what: NRCS curve number from hydrologic soil group × NLCD land cover/impervious share, AMC II, scaled and clipped; cumulative SCS-CN rain excess per cell; then a steady loss is taken out of each hour of excess.

source.text: USDA SCS (1986) Urban Hydrology for Small Watersheds, Technical Release 55
USDA NRCS National Engineering Handbook Part 630 Hydrology, Chapter 10 (2004): Estimation of direct runoff from storm rainfall
USDA NRCS Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO), hydrologic soil group
MRLC National Land Cover Database 2021 (land cover + fractional impervious surface)

symbols: cumulative rain since the start, mm

parameters.name: curve-number scale c
parameters.origin: calibrated on Leominster Sep 2023 (two USGS gauges, pre-set rule; docs/proto/parity/BASELINE.md)

parameters.name: steady loss after runoff
parameters.origin: set by us (soak-in of ponded water and minor storm drains)

parameters.name: loss taken from the hourly excess (parity mode)

nodes.output: effective rain r_eff, mm per hour per cell
nodes.limits: One global scale; the scale is below 1 although Sept 2023 was wet: it stands in for losses the model lacks.

nodes.title: Surface roughness (Manning n)
nodes.plain: Rough ground (forest) slows water down; smooth pavement and rivers let it move fast.
nodes.what: Manning n per cell: channels and open water, dense pavement (> 30 % impervious), everything else.

source.text: Chow V.T. (1959) Open-Channel Hydraulics. McGraw-Hill (Manning n tables; permissible velocities)

parameters.name: floodplain n
parameters.origin: Chow 1959 flood plains (set by us within the table range)

nodes.limits: One value per class; not calibrated.

nodes.title: Rain on every cell
nodes.plain: Each 20 m square gets its own rain for every hour: measured rain for a past storm, forecast rain for the next two days.
nodes.what: Replay: MRMS on every cell. Forecast: 12 h of observed MRMS spin-up, then HRRR (neighbourhood-spread), radar nowcast in the first hours of the issue member, snow held out. Rain minus losses → the solver’s dynamic rain file (NetCDF).

source.text: NOAA NSSL / NCEP, MRMS MultiSensor QPE 01H Pass2 (AWS noaa-mrms-pds)
NOAA GSL / NCEP, High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) v4 (AWS noaa-hrrr-bdp-pds)

nodes.limits: Hourly steps smooth out 5–15 min bursts.

nodes.title: LISFLOOD-FP 8.2 flood engine
nodes.plain: The engine moves the water downhill across the 20 m squares, a tiny step at a time, and records how deep it gets everywhere.
nodes.what: LISFLOOD-FP 8.2 (University of Bristol), 2-D local-inertial ("acceleration") solver: momentum on cell faces with Manning friction, mass continuity per cell, adaptive time step capped at 1 s; free (outflow) boundaries; CPU (OpenMP) build on GitHub Actions, CUDA build on WPI Turing (same results under the parity settings).

source.text: Bates P.D., Horritt M.S., Fewtrell T.J. (2010) A simple inertial formulation of the shallow water equations for efficient two-dimensional flood inundation modelling. J. Hydrology 387
de Almeida G.A.M., Bates P., Freer J.E., Souvignet M. (2012) Improving the stability of a simple formulation of the shallow water equations for 2-D flood modeling. Water Resources Research 48
Shaw J. et al. (2021) LISFLOOD-FP 8.0: the new discontinuous Galerkin shallow-water solver for multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Geosci. Model Dev. 14
LISFLOOD-FP 8.2 source code (Zenodo)

nodes.resolution: 20 m; time step ≤ 1 s; snapshots every 5 min
nodes.formula: \begin{gathered}q^{t+\Delta t}=\frac{q^{t}-g\,h_f\,\Delta t\,\partial(h+z)/\partial x}{1+g\,\Delta t\,n^{2}\,|q^{t}|\,/\,h_f^{7/3}}\\[6pt]\frac{h^{t+\Delta t}-h^{t}}{\Delta t}=\frac{\sum q_{\mathrm{in}}-\sum q_{\mathrm{out}}}{\Delta x}+r_{\mathrm{eff}}\\[6pt]\Delta t=\min\!\Big(\alpha\,\frac{\Delta x}{\sqrt{g\,h_{\max}}},\;\Delta t_{\max}\Big)\end{gathered}
nodes.formula_text: q⁺ = (q − g h_f Δt ∂(h+z)/∂x) / (1 + g Δt n² |q| / h_f^7/3);  Δh/Δt = Σq/Δx + r_eff;  Δt = min(α Δx/√(g h), Δt_max)
symbols: flow per unit width across a cell face, m²/s
flow depth at the face, m

parameters.name: parity settings: time-step cap Δt_max = 1 s, soil loss taken from the rain
parameters.origin: CPU/GPU parity audit: 1 s is converged (0.5 s gives the same result); docs/proto/parity/PARITY.md

parameters.name: default floodplain friction (fpfric)
parameters.origin: overridden cell by cell by the Manning map

nodes.output: water depth h(x, y, t) every 5 min; peak depth h_max; speeds; face flows
nodes.limits: No pipes, no infiltration of standing water, no sediment or debris.

nodes.title: Water depth every 5 minutes
nodes.plain: The engine’s main answer: how deep the water is on every square, every 5 minutes.
nodes.what: Depth snapshots (.wd), peak depth (.max) and the snapshot peak; stored as cm grids.
nodes.limits: A flash peak between snapshots is caught by h_max, not by the frames.

nodes.title: Water speed and flows
nodes.plain: How fast the water moves and how much flows through each road crossing.
nodes.what: Face velocities (.Vx/.Vy) → cell speed, peak depth × speed; face fluxes → flow through crossings.

parameters.name: velocity output
parameters.origin: needed by the fast-water and washout checks

nodes.output: V(x, y), d·V, Q at crossings
nodes.limits: Speeds on 20 m cells over steep verges can be numerical (capped at 5 m/s in the edge check).

nodes.title: Road sampled every 10 m
nodes.plain: We put a dot every 10 m along every road and read the water depth under each dot.
nodes.what: Road points densified every RES/2 = 10 m along each segment, mapped to the 20 m depth cell; cells lowered by hydraulic edits (notch, channel, breach) are waterway cells, not road.
nodes.limits: Lane-level position is not resolved inside a 20 m cell.

nodes.title: Road depth d (second-highest point)
nodes.plain: For each road piece we take the second-deepest dot, so one odd dot cannot close a road on its own.
nodes.what: Segment depth d = the second-highest depth over the segment’s road points (the highest when it has one point).
nodes.formula_text: d = 2nd-highest h over the segment’s road points
symbols: depth at road point p, m
nodes.limits: A short dip shorter than 20 m of road is not counted.

nodes.title: Only water the storm added
nodes.plain: Water that was already there before the rain (a stream in a culvert gap) is not counted as flooding.
nodes.what: Depth is measured above what stood on the road when the rain began (box-mean rain since start ≥ 1 mm); in forecasts a closure also needs a rise of ≥ 30 cm after onset (P1 rise rule).
nodes.limits: A road already under water before the storm is not flagged even if it gets deeper by less than 30 cm.

nodes.title: Ponding → chance of closure
nodes.plain: If the water on a road is about 30 cm deep (above a car’s door sill), the road is likely closed.
nodes.what: Closure probability from segment depth with a normal uncertainty; a segment is flagged closed when p ≥ 0.5 (i.e. d ≥ 30 cm).

parameters.name: closure depth d₀
parameters.origin: ordinary car stalls / floats around 0.3 m (Shand et al. 2011; Pregnolato et al. 2017: speed 0 at 300 mm)

parameters.name: uncertainty σ
parameters.origin: set by us (lidar + model depth error)

source.text: Shand T.D. et al. (2011) Australian Rainfall and Runoff Project 10: Appropriate Safety Criteria for Vehicles. Stage 2 report P10/S2/020
Pregnolato M., Ford A., Wilkinson S.M., Dawson R.J. (2017) The impact of flooding on road transport: a depth-disruption function. Transportation Research Part D 55

nodes.limits: Depth only: a road can fail by erosion with little ponded water.

nodes.title: Culvert capacity (HDS-5)
nodes.plain: For surveyed pipes we check whether the stream flow is bigger than the pipe can carry before water goes over the road.
nodes.what: FHWA HDS-5 inlet/outlet-control headwater for surveyed culverts (size, shape, inlet); capacity at road-crest headwater vs the modelled flow, flow uncertain by a lognormal factor; NAACC inlet blockage reduces capacity (Poor 25 %, Critical 50 %). Map layer; not part of p_close by default.
symbols: modelled peak flow at the crossing, m³/s
culvert capacity at road-crest headwater, m³/s

parameters.name: blockage, NAACC "Poor"
parameters.origin: ARR 2019 Book 6 ch. 6 design blockage range

source.text: Schall J.D. et al. (2012) Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts, 3rd ed. FHWA-HIF-12-026 (HDS-5)
Ball J. et al. (eds) (2019) Australian Rainfall and Runoff: A Guide to Flood Estimation, Book 6 (blockage ch. 6; safety design criteria ch. 7)
North Atlantic Aquatic Connectivity Collaborative (NAACC) road-stream crossing surveys

nodes.limits: Only surveyed culverts; debris during the storm is not predicted.

nodes.title: Freeboard (water beside the road)
nodes.plain: If the water next to the road comes within 30 cm of the road top, the road edge is at risk.
nodes.what: Freeboard f = road crest − highest water surface within 30 m; design practice keeps 1 ft (0.30 m) of freeboard; σ combines lidar and model height errors.

parameters.name: design freeboard m
parameters.origin: 1 ft freeboard of DOT culvert/ditch criteria under HDS-5

source.text: Schall J.D. et al. (2012) Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts, 3rd ed. FHWA-HIF-12-026 (HDS-5)
USGS Lidar Base Specification (quality level 2: RMSEz ≤ 10 cm)

nodes.limits: Uses peak water surface, not duration.

nodes.title: Depth × speed (vehicle stability)
nodes.plain: Even shallow water can push a car off the road if it moves fast enough.
nodes.what: Peak depth × speed against the small-car stability limit of the ARR vehicle-safety criteria.

parameters.name: small-car limit d·V
parameters.origin: Shand et al. 2011 / ARR 2019 Book 6 ch. 7 (H1/H2)

parameters.name: σ (log)
parameters.origin: half the log-range of the vehicle classes

source.text: Shand T.D. et al. (2011) Australian Rainfall and Runoff Project 10: Appropriate Safety Criteria for Vehicles. Stage 2 report P10/S2/020
Ball J. et al. (eds) (2019) Australian Rainfall and Runoff: A Guide to Flood Estimation, Book 6 (blockage ch. 6; safety design criteria ch. 7)

nodes.limits: Snapshot speeds every 5 min can miss short spikes.

nodes.title: Embankment washout at crossings
nodes.plain: When water pours over a road at a stream crossing fast enough, it can wash the road fill away.
nodes.what: Overtopping speed on unedited road cells near a crossing vs the permissible velocity of grass on easily eroded soil.

source.text: Chow V.T. (1959) Open-Channel Hydraulics. McGraw-Hill (Manning n tables; permissible velocities)

nodes.limits: No soil or embankment data; one permissible velocity for all fills.

nodes.title: Edge erosion along the road
nodes.plain: Fast, shallow water running along a road can wash out the gravel shoulder even without a deep puddle.
nodes.what: Both a speed and a shear criterion must be exceeded beside the road (HEC-15 τ = γ h S vs gravel permissible shear), weighted by time above 1 m/s.

parameters.name: reference duration
parameters.origin: CIRIA R116 (Hewlett et al. 1987) duration curves

source.text: Kilgore R.T., Cotton G.K. (2005) Design of Roadside Channels with Flexible Linings. FHWA-IF-05-114 (HEC-15)
Chow V.T. (1959) Open-Channel Hydraulics. McGraw-Hill (Manning n tables; permissible velocities)

nodes.status: candidate layer (opt-in; adds +0 Leominster DPW sites)
nodes.limits: A 20 m grid cannot hold the curb-line flow that causes most edge washouts.

nodes.title: Road network graph
nodes.plain: All road pieces joined at junctions, so we can find routes like a GPS does.
nodes.what: District 3 MassDOT graph; free-flow travel time per segment by class; a closed segment is removed, a wet one slowed.

source.text: MassDOT Road Inventory (segments, functional class, AADT) via the MassDOT open-data portal

nodes.limits: Daily traffic only (flat profile); no traffic assignment.

nodes.title: Slower on wet roads (Pregnolato curve)
nodes.plain: Cars drive slower through water; at 30 cm they stop.
nodes.what: Speed reduction by depth (5–30 cm) from the depth–disruption function.

source.text: Pregnolato M., Ford A., Wilkinson S.M., Dawson R.J. (2017) The impact of flooding on road transport: a depth-disruption function. Transportation Research Part D 55

nodes.output: speed factor per segment and frame
nodes.limits: Fitted on UK data.

nodes.title: Shortest routes and detours
nodes.plain: The computer finds the quickest way around closed roads, like a navigation app.
nodes.what: Dijkstra shortest paths on the wet graph (node-weighted by travel time); detours capped at 30 min; vehicle-hours from AADT.

source.text: Dijkstra E.W. (1959) A note on two problems in connexion with graphs. Numerische Mathematik 1

nodes.limits: No congestion feedback (no equilibrium assignment).

nodes.title: Emergency access standards
nodes.plain: We count people who can no longer reach a hospital in 30 min, a fire station in 8 min or police in 10 min.
nodes.what: Residents within the standard of an open facility, now vs dry; isolated = no route to any open hospital, fire or police station.

parameters.name: hospital
parameters.origin: Carr et al. 2009 (share within 30 min of an emergency department)

parameters.name: police
parameters.origin: set by us (no national standard; planning assumption)

source.text: Carr B.G. et al. (2009) Access to emergency care in the United States. Annals of Emergency Medicine 54(2)
NFPA 1710 (2020) Standard for the Organization and Deployment of Fire Suppression Operations… (§4.1.2.1.1: 480 s travel, full first alarm)
US Census Bureau, 2020 Census blocks (TIGER/Line + P1 population)
OpenStreetMap contributors (hospitals, fire and police stations, via Overpass)

nodes.limits: Night-time population; facilities from OSM.

nodes.title: Network resilience (efficiency)
nodes.plain: One number for how well the whole road network still moves people during the storm.
nodes.what: Global efficiency of the network over time, as used for road-network resilience by Ganin et al. 2017.

source.text: Latora V., Marchiori M. (2001) Efficient behavior of small-world networks. Physical Review Letters 87
Ganin A.A. et al. (2017) Resilience and efficiency in transportation networks. Science Advances 3(12) e1701079

symbols: shortest travel time from i to j
nodes.status: live in replays (skipped in the forecast for speed)
nodes.limits: All trips weighted equally.

nodes.title: Rain gate
nodes.plain: The flood model only runs for real when the forecast shows heavy rain somewhere in the district.
nodes.what: Any District 3 town with forecast 6 h maximum ≥ 25 mm or 24 h maximum ≥ 40 mm (HRRR); then up to 4 boxes of 20 × 20 km on the wettest towns. Below that, rain ≥ 8 mm still runs one box ("water mode", never a warning).

parameters.name: 6 h threshold G₆
parameters.origin: every catalogue closure storm must fire it (docs/proto/forecast/GATE.md)

nodes.limits: HRRR intensity errors pass straight into the gate.

nodes.title: Spreading the forecast (20 km / 90th percentile)
nodes.plain: Because forecasts often put the storm a little off, each spot takes the heavier rain forecast near it.
nodes.what: Each HRRR value replaced by the 90th percentile within 20 km, every hour (neighbourhood approach).

source.text: Schwartz C.S., Sobash R.A. (2017) Generating probabilistic forecasts from convection-allowing ensembles using neighborhood approaches: a review and recommendations. Monthly Weather Review 145

nodes.limits: Adds rain volume (deliberate: catches displaced cores).

nodes.title: Radar spin-up + nowcast
nodes.plain: The forecast starts from the rain that has already fallen, and uses radar for the first hours.
nodes.what: 12 h of observed MRMS before the cycle; for the issue member the first hours are observed / radar-advected nowcast, blended into HRRR.

source.text: NOAA NSSL / NCEP, MRMS MultiSensor QPE 01H Pass2 (AWS noaa-mrms-pds)

nodes.limits: Nowcast skill fades after ~2 h.

nodes.title: Rain or snow
nodes.plain: When it is cold, part of the precipitation falls as snow and does not run off right away.
nodes.what: Liquid fraction from HRRR 2 m temperature, linear between 0 and 2 °C; frozen part kept as snow (no melt within the run).
nodes.limits: No snowmelt; no rain-on-snow.

nodes.title: 8 time-lagged HRRR members
nodes.plain: We run the flood model with the newest forecast and 7 slightly older ones, to see how much they agree.
nodes.what: Members T, T−6, T−12, T−18 h (48 h cycles) plus the hourly cycles before T; each is its own flood run per box; older members reused from cache.
nodes.limits: Lagged members share the same model errors.

nodes.title: "k of 8": likely / possible
nodes.plain: A road is "likely closed" if at least 2 of the 8 runs close it, "possible" if 1 does.
nodes.what: k = number of members with p_close ≥ 0.5 on the segment; likely k ≥ 2, possible k = 1. Shown as "k of 8", not as a percentage.
nodes.limits: Members can agree on a wrong storm position.

nodes.title: Ranking by chance of flooding (π)
nodes.plain: Roads in the list are ordered by how likely they are to really flood, using depth and a few road and rain facts.
nodes.what: π from a fitted logistic model on the deployed depth probit plus hazard terms (hours > 15 cm, HAND, slope, culvert/overtop/sag/edge layers, peak 1 h rain, stream distance, length); used for order only. Not shown as a %: used for order only until its calibration is proven.

source.text: Bekker J., Davis J. (2020) Learning from positive and unlabeled data: a survey. Machine Learning 109

nodes.limits: Fitted on reports, which favour busy roads.

nodes.title: Flood reports (labels, never inputs)
nodes.plain: Real reports of flooded roads are kept aside and used only to check the model, never to feed it.
nodes.what: NWS Local Storm Reports, NOAA Storm Events, MassDOT roadway events, news / WX1BOX, Leominster DPW damage points, (opt-in) SeeClickFix and crash records. Positive-unlabelled: a road with no report is not a dry road.

source.text: NWS Local Storm Reports (Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive)
NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database
MassDOT / Mass511 traveler information (roadway events)
City of Leominster DPW, Sept 2023 flash-flood damage points (shared with the project, Oct 2026)
Bekker J., Davis J. (2020) Learning from positive and unlabeled data: a survey. Machine Learning 109

nodes.limits: Reports cluster on busy roads; most flooded roads are never reported.

nodes.title: Matching reports to roads
nodes.plain: A report counts for a road if it is within 30 m of it; reports close together count once.
nodes.what: Strict match within 30 m of a road point; labels clustered single-link within 150 m into sites; approximate locations carry a position uncertainty.
nodes.limits: Approximate coordinates (~500 m) limit what can be matched.

nodes.title: Scores
nodes.plain: We ask: of the real flooded places, how many were on the model’s short list, compared with picking roads at random?
nodes.what: Site recall at the closure rule and at fixed shares (top 1–10 % of segments); chance recall (exact hypergeometric) and lift; CSI; FSS at 100/300/1000 m; storm-clustered bootstrap CIs; paired tests with pre-registered adoption rules.

source.text: Roberts N.M., Lean H.W. (2008) Scale-selective verification of rainfall accumulations from high-resolution forecasts of convective events. Monthly Weather Review 136

nodes.formula_text: recall@k% = sites hit / sites;  lift = recall / chance;  CSI = H/(H+M+F)
nodes.output: skill (reported elsewhere, not on this tree)
nodes.limits: Few sites per storm; wide intervals.

nodes.title: Six named baselines
nodes.plain: The model must beat simple alternatives an office could use today.
nodes.what: NWS flash-flood warnings; FEMA 100-yr zone; MassDOT repeat flood points; radar rain threshold; terrain only (HAND); static hazard × vulnerability × consequence.

source.text: NWS flash-flood warnings (IEM VTEC archive)
FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (100-year zone)

nodes.limits: Some baselines are undated (used for every storm).

nodes.title: Calibration vs test storms
nodes.plain: One storm was used to set the model; all the others are tests it never saw.
nodes.what: Calibration: Leominster Sep 2023 (and Worcester Aug 2021 for design choices). Tests: 23 held-out District 3 storms, 81 District 4–6 storms (frozen settings), the live forward test from 3 Nov 2026. 5 locked storms never opened.
nodes.limits: The test set is small in District 3.

nodes.title: River gauges
nodes.plain: River-level gauges show whether the model’s rivers rise as much and as early as the real ones.
nodes.what: USGS 15-min stage; modelled rise at the nearest channel cell vs observed rise and peak time.

source.text: USGS Water Data for the Nation (stream stage, 15-min)

nodes.limits: Few gauges per box; small streams ungauged.

nodes.title: Culverts blocked 0–100 %
nodes.plain: What if the pipes under the roads were partly or fully clogged with debris?
nodes.what: Culvert notch floor raised by a fraction f of the opening (f = 1: solid fill); bridges stay open; optionally only the smallest third of surveyed culverts.

source.text: Ball J. et al. (eds) (2019) Australian Rainfall and Runoff: A Guide to Flood Estimation, Book 6 (blockage ch. 6; safety design criteria ch. 7)

nodes.limits: Geometric proxy for an inlet-area reduction.

nodes.title: Dry / wet soil (AMC I / III)
nodes.plain: What if the ground was already soaked (or bone dry) before the storm?
nodes.what: Curve number converted to antecedent class I or III (Chow et al. 1988), calibration scale kept.

source.text: USDA NRCS National Engineering Handbook Part 630 Hydrology, Chapter 10 (2004): Estimation of direct runoff from storm rainfall
Chow V.T., Maidment D.R., Mays L.W. (1988) Applied Hydrology. McGraw-Hill (antecedent-moisture CN conversions)

nodes.limits: One class for the whole box.

nodes.title: Frozen ground
nodes.plain: What if the same storm hit frozen ground in early spring, when water cannot soak in?
nodes.what: Knisel (CREAMS) rule: CN 95 where the unfrozen CN ≤ 80, else 98; no steady soak-in.

source.text: Knisel W.G. (ed.) (1980) CREAMS: A Field-Scale Model for Chemicals, Runoff and Erosion from Agricultural Management Systems. USDA Conservation Research Report 26 (frozen-soil curve number)

nodes.limits: Real frost varies with snow cover and depth.

nodes.title: More or less rain
nodes.plain: What if the same storm had been half as strong, or a quarter stronger?
nodes.what: Every hour of the observed radar rain multiplied (× 0.5 to × 1.25), same timing and place.
nodes.limits: Scaling keeps the storm’s shape.

nodes.title: Edge erosion without ponding
nodes.plain: Roads that wash out at the edge with almost no standing water are missed.
nodes.what: Most missed Leominster damage (Sep 2023) is edge washout with ~2 cm of modelled water, mostly along one street; curb-line flow is narrower than a 20 m cell.
nodes.limits: Needs curb-line flow and damage inventories from more towns.

nodes.title: Debris blockage during the storm
nodes.plain: Branches and trash that clog a pipe during the storm are not predicted.
nodes.what: Blockage can be imposed as a what-if, not forecast.
nodes.limits: No debris-supply data.

nodes.title: Storm drains (pipes)
nodes.plain: City storm-drain pipes are not in the model yet.
nodes.what: Street inlets and pipes carry part of the runoff in built-up areas; the model has no pipe network.
nodes.limits: Pipe network data (sizes, inverts, condition) are held by each city.

nodes.title: Groundwater
nodes.plain: Rising groundwater under roads and foundations is not modelled.
nodes.what: No subsurface flow; antecedent wetness only through the curve number.
nodes.limits: Needs groundwater observations.
